abstract: Microalgae are nutrient-dense food sources with elemental compositions that have potential in addressing micronutrient deficiencies. In particular, Limnospira platensis and Chlorella vulgaris are recognized for the potential high contribution they could have in mineral intake, including Fe, Ca and Mg. However, most nutritional profiling of microalgae biomass relies on bulk measurements without resolving intercellular differences in elemental content. In this study, argon-sustained and nitrogen-based plasma time-of-flight mass spectrometry (TOFMS) was employed to achieve single-cell quantification of elemental fingerprints in morphologically distinct L. platensis and C. vulgaris, cultivated autotrophically in standard and iron-enriched media, with C. vulgaris additionally grown in mixotrophic conditions. The size limitation of transporting cells >10 µm into inductively-coupled plasma (ICP) was addressed by using a gravity-assisted sampling method that delivers microdroplets containing large L. platensis filaments into ICP for high-resolution elemental profiling at the single-cell level. Bulk measurements validated overall elemental trends, whereas single-cell analysis resolved intercellular distributions. Nutritionally and physiologically relevant elements, including Fe, Mg, Ca, Cu, P, K, and Mn, were successfully quantified at picogram-to-femtogram per-cell levels, highlighting the multi-element capability of single-cell ICP-TOFMS. Iron enrichment induced a pronounced increase in cellular iron content from 0.5 to 1.5 pg/cell in L. platensis. In contrast, C. vulgaris maintained a stable single-cell elemental profile across standard and iron-enriched media, with iron contents of 3.9 and 3.6 fg/cell, respectively. This work expands the applicability of ICP-TOFMS for multi-element single-cell analysis of morphologically diverse microalgae, opening new possibilities to link cultivation conditions with cellular mineral accumulation and nutritional value.
